## `fetch(url, options)`

Since Next.js extends the [Web `fetch()` API](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Fetch_API), you can use any of the [native options available](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/fetch#parameters).

### `options.cache`

Configure how the request should interact with Next.js [caching](/docs/app/getting-started/caching).

```ts
fetch(`https://...`, { cache: 'force-cache' | 'no-store' })
```

- **`auto no cache`** (default): Next.js fetches the resource from the remote server on every request in development, but will fetch once during `next build` because the route will be statically prerendered. If [Request-time APIs](/docs/app/glossary#request-time-apis) are detected on the route, Next.js will fetch the resource on every request.
- **`no-store`**: Next.js fetches the resource from the remote server on every request, even if Request-time APIs are not detected on the route.
- **`force-cache`**: Next.js looks for a matching request in its server-side cache. A request matches on its URL, method, headers, and body, so requests that differ in any of these are cached separately.
  - If there is a match and it is fresh, it will be returned from the cache.
  - If there is no match or a stale match, Next.js fetches the resource from the remote server and updates the cache with the downloaded resource. Only responses with a `200` HTTP status code are stored.

> **Good to know**: Caching is opt-in. Set `cache: 'force-cache'` to cache any request, including `POST` and requests that send `authorization` or `cookie` headers. [Draft Mode](/docs/app/guides/draft-mode) bypasses the cache entirely (no read or write).

### `options.next.revalidate`

```ts
fetch(`https://...`, { next: { revalidate: false | 0 | number } })
```

Set the cache lifetime of a resource (in seconds).

- **`false`** - Cache the resource indefinitely. Semantically equivalent to `revalidate: Infinity`. The HTTP cache may evict older resources over time.
- **`0`** - Prevent the resource from being cached.
- **`number`** - (in seconds) Specify the resource should have a cache lifetime of at most `n` seconds.

> **Good to know**:
>
> - If an individual `fetch()` request sets a `revalidate` number lower than the [default `revalidate`](/docs/app/guides/caching-without-cache-components#route-segment-config-revalidate) of a route, the whole route revalidation interval will be decreased.
> - If two fetch requests with the same URL in the same route have different `revalidate` values, the lower value will be used.

content.text:
`UserDashboard` is now an async server component that fetches user preferences fresh on every request. The only file I changed is `app/UserDashboard.tsx`.

**What it does**

- `getUserPreferences()` is a separate async helper that calls `fetch('https://api.example.com/user/preferences', { cache: 'no-store' })`, mirroring the `getStaticData()` helper in `app/page.tsx`. Like that helper, it wraps the call in `try/catch` and returns a fallback (`{}`) so the page still renders if the API is unreachable, and it also treats non-2xx responses as failures.
- `export default async function UserDashboard()` awaits the helper and renders the theme, language, and notification settings with sensible defaults when a field is missing.

**Why `cache: 'no-store'` matters**

In the installed Next.js (16.4 canary), a fetch with no cache option runs once at `next build` and the route is statically prerendered. Since this data is user-specific and changes per request, `cache: 'no-store'` forces the fetch on every request and opts the route into dynamic rendering. The build output confirms this: `/` is now listed as `ƒ (Dynamic) server-rendered on demand`, whereas before it would have been static.

**Verification**

- `tsc --noEmit` passes.
- `next build` compiles and typechecks successfully.
- The build auto-reformatted `tsconfig.json` and generated `.next/`, `next-env.d.ts`, and `tsconfig.tsbuildinfo`; I reverted/removed those so the working tree only contains the intended change (plus the pre-existing `package.json` / `package-lock.json` modifications that were already there before I started).

One thing to note: `api.example.com` isn't a real endpoint, so at runtime the component will currently show the fallback values (`default` / `en` / `disabled`) until it points at a real API. If the real endpoint needs auth (cookies or headers), that's where you'd add `headers()`/`cookies()` from `next/headers` inside the helper.
